passages.where: After rescuing Lot, Abram is blessed by Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, and gives him a tenth of everything. The site's note calls it the Bible's first tithe, given freely before any law required it, a confession that the spoils came from God. The plain note asks what you give back to God, and whether you give it gladly.

Every third year the tithe is stored in the towns so that the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow may come and eat their fill. The site's note on the chapter says the tithe was eaten in joy before God, and every third year became a food bank for those with no land of their own. Israel's giving fed both those who served at the sanctuary and those with nothing.

When Hezekiah calls the people to support the priests and Levites, they bring firstfruits and tithes so generously that heaps pile up for four months. The site's note on the chapter says the people were to give their first and best, support those who serve in ministry, and handle the gifts faithfully, and that Hezekiah appointed faithful Levites to distribute them fairly. Generous giving and honest handling belong together.

The people bring freewill offerings for the tabernacle morning after morning, until Moses has to send word through the camp for them to stop. The site's note on the chapter says the offerings kept coming until Moses told the camp to stop giving. The gifts were freewill offerings, brought morning after morning by people no one had to press.

Jesus tells his disciples that a poor widow who put in two small coins has given more than all the rich, because she gave all she had to live on. The site's plain note says most readers hear praise of her costly devotion, while some, following Addison Wright, hear Jesus lament a system that taught a poor woman to give her last coins, since he has just condemned those who devour widows' houses; many now hold both. It says the story does not teach that the poor must give away what they need to live, or that God's favour can be bought.

Paul asks each believer to set aside a portion of income on the first day of every week for the poor believers in Jerusalem. The site's plain note says no rule of amount is given here: Paul asks for giving that is regular, planned and in proportion to what each one has. It asks whether your giving is planned, or only left to the moment.

If the eagerness is there, Paul says, the gift is acceptable according to what one has, not according to what one does not have. The site's plain note on 1 Corinthians 16 quotes this verse to show that Paul asks for giving in proportion. A small gift from little is not a small gift.

Paul says the Lord has directed that those who preach the gospel should receive their living from it, and then explains why he himself set the right aside. The site's plain note says most churches pay their ministers for that reason and nothing here counts it wrong, that a minister may choose not to use the right, and that nothing here gives anyone licence to demand money for the gospel or grow rich from it. It asks whether those who serve you are cared for as Paul says they should be.

Thanking the Philippians for their gift, Paul calls it a fragrant offering, an acceptable sacrifice, well pleasing to God. The site's plain note says the church had given out of its own poverty, not as an investment, and asks whether you would see helping someone this week as an offering to God. A gift to God's work is worship before it is funding.

Jesus rebukes leaders who tithe even kitchen herbs and neglect the weightier matters of the law, justice, mercy and faithfulness, and says they should have done both. The site's note says careful obedience in small things is commended, not dismissed, but small obedience that becomes a substitute for the great is condemned. The plain note asks what your mint and dill are, the habits that make you feel faithful.

misread.taken: Give, and it will be given to you, pressed down and running over, is used to promise that money given to a church or ministry will come back as more money.
misread.says: The site's plain note says verse 38 is sometimes used to promise money in return for giving money, often to a ministry, and that this is not what it means. The setting is mercy, forgiveness and lending to enemies without expecting anything back, and God's overflowing measure is his mercy, not a payout. The plain note on Philippians 4 says that if you gave because you were pressed or frightened, or promised a return that never came, that was not your failure; you were not lacking in faith, and the promise was wrong.

differ.share: Christians agree that everything a person has comes from God, that giving should be generous and glad and never forced, that God's people are to give their first and best and support those who serve in ministry, that gifts must be handled faithfully, and that giving is never a technique for getting rich.

views.name: A tenth as the standard
views.body: Some Christians hold that the tithe is still the pattern for God's people, because it predates the law of Moses: Abram gave a tenth to Melchizedek and Jacob vowed one, and Jesus affirmed tithing in passing in Matthew 23:23.

views.name: Generous, proportionate giving without a fixed percentage
views.body: Others hold that the tithe belonged to Israel's temple system, which Christ fulfilled, and that the New Testament replaces a fixed percentage with generous, cheerful giving in proportion to what each one has (2 Corinthians 8 and 9), which may be more or less than a tenth.

differ.after: The site's notes on Genesis 14, 2 Chronicles 31, Malachi 3 and 1 Corinthians 16 set out both views and do not settle it; the note on 2 Chronicles 31 calls it a second-order question on which faithful believers differ.

whole: Giving to a church raises questions people are often too embarrassed to ask. How much? A tenth of what, before tax or after? What if we cannot afford it this year? What if I do not trust how the money is used? Some were raised with the tithe as a fixed rule and feel guilty whenever they fall short. Some have been pressed for money by preachers who promised it would come back many times over, and gave what they could not afford. Some give nothing, not from greed but from never having been taught, and some give generously and quietly and never think about it at all.

Scripture treats giving to God's work as worship, and it is honest about how it goes wrong. Abram's tenth was a confession that his victory came from God; the Philippians' gift was a fragrant offering; Israel's tithe fed the Levites and, every third year, the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow. But Jesus rebuked leaders who tithed their herbs and neglected justice, mercy and faithfulness, and he spoke against those who devour widows' houses just before he watched a poor widow give her last coins. The danger runs both ways: a hand closed against God's work, and a religion that takes from the poor or sells blessing for money. The prosperity promise that giving buys wealth, which the site's notes call an error, turns grace into a transaction.

So the Bible's wisdom is to give on purpose and with a free heart. Set something aside regularly, as Paul asked, in proportion to what you have, knowing that a gift is acceptable according to what one has and not what one lacks. Support those who teach and serve you, as Paul says the Lord directed, and expect the church to handle what you give faithfully, as Hezekiah appointed faithful men to distribute the tithes. Whether you take a tenth as your standard or give without a fixed percentage, faithful Christians stand on both sides of that question, and neither side allows giving to be forced. If you are in money trouble, the plain note on Philippians 4 says to look for a trusted adviser where you live, and the plain note on Mark 12 says no one is taught to give away what they need to live.

The hope Scripture gives is that God is not a fundraiser. Christ, though rich, became poor for our sake, as the plain note on 2 Corinthians 8 puts it, and the church's offering is a response to that gift, not a payment toward it. Once, the people of Israel gave so freely that Moses had to tell them to stop. That is what giving looks like when it comes from glad hearts rather than pressure, and it is still possible.
sit: Is your giving planned, glad and in proportion to what you have, and if not, what is one step toward that this month?

prayer.lead: The site's plain note says Psalm 96 asks what people treat as gods, money among them, and answers not with anger but with an invitation to worship the one who made the heavens. Pray these lines when you give.
